content_voiceover: These two board questions test the genetics and epidemiology of hemophilia A and B. Both conditions are X-linked recessive disorders, but roughly a third of newly diagnosed patients have no family history at all, because the mutation arose de novo in the fertilized egg, meaning the mother is not necessarily a carrier. Severe disease accounts for close to half of all hemophilia A cases, not a small minority. An important clinical pearl is that even mild or moderate hemophilia A patients can develop factor eight inhibitors, which converts their bleeding pattern into something that behaves clinically like severe disease. On genetics, intron twenty two inversion is the single most common molecular defect in severe hemophilia A, explaining almost half of severe cases, while gross gene rearrangements are comparatively uncommon in hemophilia B. Hemophilia B more typically arises from missense point mutations rather than nonsense mutations, and the Leyden variant specifically involves disruption of the proximal promoter of the F9 gene. Overall, hemophilia A remains both more prevalent and generally more severe than hemophilia B.
keypoints: Both hemophilia A and B are X-linked recessive
About a third of cases are de novo, no family history
Severe disease is about half of hemophilia A cases
Intron 22 inversion is the top cause of severe hemophilia A
Hemophilia B usually involves missense, not nonsense, mutations
